Purpose","sectionText":"## 1. Purpose

Holder-lock answers one question for every cold lock in fgOS: who holds this resource right now, as the kernel sees it. A lock is a kernel lock on an open file description. The kernel releases it when every process holding a copy of that description has died, so no decision anywhere in the component is derived from a pid, a TTL, a start time or an mtime. The one pid the component reads is the locker identity the kernel itself stamps on a lock record (`flock` stores the calling process's pid on the description's lock); it is compared only against this live process's own pid, never used to infer liveness or ownership of a record.

Every caller (the Node facade, a Rust crate, a git hook) goes through one port with one set of operations. Each operating system has one driver behind the port, and the port reports the guarantee level that driver gives on the filesystem the lock files live on. Nothing in the public interface is POSIX-only: a caller never sees a file descriptor or a handle of the operating system.

The component owns the cold locks, the main checkout mutex, the merge slot and `worktree-admin` (sections 14 and 16). The state store's hot mutex (`state`, `porting-events`) is built on the same facade for its cleanup lock but is implemented by the state store, not by this component (section 15)."},{"unitKind":"unheaded-block","anchor":"unheaded-block-2","githubAnchor":"unheaded-block-2","stableAnchor":"unheaded-block-2","title":"Unheaded block 2","startLine":27,"endLine":27,"textDigest":"9290f9b1124b0c7a8aa9a822860257698b6e1c0a0a4ccb18b855caf1e3c7aa56","sample":"Holder-lock answers one question for every cold lock in fgOS: who holds this resource right now, as the kernel sees it. | Owns | Does not own |

| The port: `acquire`, `release`, `run_borrowed`, `probe`, `holders`, `guarantee` ([contract](../../../packages/holder-lock/contracts/holder-lock.port.v1.json)) | Writer identity (Session Identity) |

| The lock registry: every lock's name, kind, scope, rank and path ([registry](../../../packages/holder-lock/contracts/lock-registry.v1.json)) | The attempt lock's lifecycle (run supervisor) and the containment port (process control) |
| The single state-root resolution and `lockRoot` (section 11) | The meaning of a lock's contents (a lock file is never read for data) |
| The in-process door (section 9) and the internal routes `fgos internal lock-fd` (borrowed check and shared try only), `lock-hold`, `quiesce-scan`, `lock-borrow-vectors` (section 10) | Any verb a person calls |

There is one implementation of the primitive, the Rust crate `fgos-holder-lock`, which calls `flock` in process. The Node facade in `src/holder-lock/` opens the lock file itself and passes the open description to the door (`holderLock.lockFd`), which locks it in the same process; Node keeps the descriptor, the door keeps a duplicate and the creation marks beside it, and the lock stays with the description. On Windows the lock is held by a `lock-hold` helper process instead, because `LockFileEx` belongs to the process that took it. Rust and Node lock the same file with the same primitive, so a Rust writer and a Node writer exclude each other with no second protocol.

The port","sectionText":"## 3. The port

Operations, as the contract states them:

| Operation | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `acquire(resource, mode: EX \| SH, wait: try \| ms N, killWaitMs)` | Hold the lock. Returns `acquired` with an opaque handle, `held` (reason `kernel-lock-held` or `predecessor-domain-not-empty`, with the holders when they are listable), `timeout` with the milliseconds waited, or `unavailable` (`unsupported-platform`, `unsupported-filesystem`, `host-version-mismatch`, `io-error`). `acquired` is returned only when both hold: the kernel lock is held and the predecessor domain recorded next to the lock file is empty (section 8). A free kernel lock alone is not proof |
| `clear_domain(handle)` | Recorded handoff: while holding an idle exclusive acquired handle, observe its own domain empty without killing, then remove the unchanged predecessor record. Node: `handle.clearDomain()`. Execution attaches `custody-handoff-not-recorded` to its returned settled result if this fails, retaining its original outcome. Failure preserves the record; a replaced resource refuses |
| `release(handle)` | Close every copy of the description the handle owns. The holder releases only after its own domain is empty (section 8, step 0) |
| `run_borrowed(handle, spec)` | The only way a child command (a git commit of a checkpoint or merge) runs with the holder's authority. The description goes to exactly one child through an explicit fd mapping (slot 3 by default, env `FGOS_LOCK_FD=<name>:3`). When the command is git, `-c gc.auto=0 -c maintenance.auto=false` is prepended. After the child exits the leftovers in the domain are killed and the call waits for the domain to be empty before it returns `{exit, signal, leftoversKilled}` |
| `run_borrowed_io(handle, spec, io)` | Synchronous member of `run_borrowed` with binary stdin, bounded captured stdout/stderr and an absolute monotonic deadline; returns captured bytes and the ordinary borrow outcome after cleanup. Unix only; Windows refuses `borrow-io-unsupported` before spawn and retains existing `run_borrowed` behavior |
| `probe(resource)` | One non-blocking `LOCK_SH` attempt on a fresh description, dropped at once; answers `free` or `held` and never obstructs a holder. Used by the adopt scan, the resume guard and reconcile |
| `holders(resource)` | Diagnostic list `[{pid, startTime, cmdline}]` of every process holding a description of the lock file, or `unlistable` with a reason. Linux reads `/proc/*/fdinfo/*` for a `lock:` line on the file's inode; macOS and Windows report `unlistable` |
| `guarantee(path)` | `{driver, exclusion, borrow, holders, platform, notes}` for the directory the lock files live in. The levels are `kernel`, `kernel-unmeasured`, `job-scoped`, `unsupported`, `none` |

Invariants of every result:

- `held` and `timeout` never leave a description open: the lock is released before the result is returned, and `predecessor-domain-not-empty` is returned after the kernel lock was released again.
- No result of any operation is derived from a pid, a TTL or an mtime.
- A handle is opaque. The fd lives only inside the driver; `run_borrowed` is the one place that maps it into a child.

The lock file of a resource is created once and never removed while the resource lives. A lock whose resource is a run (`attempt`, `advance`, `recovery`) lives in the run directory and goes away with the run; the inode check in section 5 makes that safe."},{"unitKind":"unheaded-block","anchor":"unheaded-block-8","githubAnchor":"unheaded-block-8","stableAnchor":"unheaded-block-8","title":"Unheaded block 8","startLine":50,"endLine":50,"textDigest":"0361cab026f7503915907b569cc19e3eb54d9f519f3edbdc9033b5f7b0328c03","sample":"Operations, as the contract states them:","identityFingerprint":"f07a6387d5b7fefdd47ba2cf4aa111efe686dab3dd0e008b9b141a589ab4507d","ancestry":["Holder-lock Component Specification","3. Description rules","sectionText":"## 5. Description rules

The boundary between right and wrong moved from "who is alive" to "who holds a copy of the description". These rules are mandatory and have tests:

1. The lock description is always `FD_CLOEXEC`. The one moment it is not is inside exactly one spawn that borrows it, through an explicit fd mapping (Node: a `stdio` slot; Rust: `dup2` in `pre_exec`).
2. The receiver (inherited fd 3, or `SCM_RIGHTS` with `MSG_CMSG_CLOEXEC`) sets `FD_CLOEXEC` before any other syscall.
3. Reason, with evidence: Node opens with `O_CLOEXEC`, but Rust's `std::process::Command` inherits every fd above 2 that is not `CLOEXEC`. Every Rust route that receives a description has a leak test: after the child ran, `/proc/<child>/fd` and a grandchild's fd table do not contain the lock inode.
4. After acquire, `fstat(fd).ino` must equal `stat(path).ino`; otherwise close and retry. This is what lets a lock file be removed with its resource.
5. The lock file is opened `O_RDWR` (NFSv4 and BSD refuse an exclusive lock on a read-only fd).
6. Borrowing is a strong right and is close-only: any copy that calls `LOCK_UN` releases the shared lock, so owner and borrower only `close`; no library guard that unlocks on drop is used. The one exception is a probe description opened and closed inside a single call (the release probe and `probe`): it is never shared, borrowed or handed on, so it is unlocked just before it is closed, which keeps a child forked by another thread in that window from inheriting its lock.
7. The doctor check `lock-holders` reports every holder that is not an fgOS process, so a violation shows up at once. The bwrap monitor process of an attempt whose supervisor or gate holds the lock is a member, not a stranger.
8. The borrow vectors are mandatory and there is no run-time switch that disables borrowing (such a switch would block fgOS's own commits and trip after every release). The vectors run in a throwaway repository with real git: a git alias that starts a background shell process, a clean/smudge filter that starts a background process, a hook that starts a background process, and `gc.auto=1` with enough loose objects; each asserts the lock is free as soon as git has exited and the owner closed its description, plus the sibling check (a process with the same `FGOS_LOCK_FD` value that opened the file itself is not a borrower). A red vector is a doctor FAIL (`lock-borrow-vectors`) and `fgctl` refuses to activate.

The borrower test used by a hook has three conditions, all required: `FGOS_LOCK_FD` names exactly the slot, `fstat(slot)` has the same `dev:ino` as the lock file, and `LOCK_EX | LOCK_NB` on the slot succeeds (a description that already holds the lock succeeds; a sibling that opened the file itself fails). Missing any one, the hook tries the lock once on a description of its own and never claims to be a borrower. The worker base env of a dispatch scrubs `FGOS_LOCK_FD` and `FGOS_MAIN_LOCK_HOLDER_PID`; a leaked variable is useless without the description.

Node synchronous `runBorrowed` accepts a positive `spec.maxOutputBytes` per captured stream (default 16 MiB); commit children request 64 MiB. Both transports refuse overflow rather than returning truncated output. The fd transport also completes leftover cleanup before reporting capture failure."},{"unitKind":"unheaded-block","anchor":"unheaded-block-16","githubAnchor":"unheaded-block-16","stableAnchor":"unheaded-block-16","title":"Unheaded block 16","startLine":86,"endLine":86,"textDigest":"4532635962c4ed3b991b2201f2f66b5d6e0f190b952487fa5b58b3bbff47d7a6","sample":"The boundary between right and wrong moved from "who is alive" to "who holds a copy of the description". Description rules"],"text":"### Explicit I/O borrowing","sectionText":"### Explicit I/O borrowing

**Extended 2026-10-18 for Git Publication: run_borrowed with explicit input, bounded capture and deadline; same lifecycle as run_borrowed.** `run_borrowed_io(&Handle, &BorrowSpec, &BorrowIo)` borrows an exclusive opaque handle for the entire synchronous call. `BorrowIo` supplies binary stdin (EOF after its last byte), independent stdout/stderr byte ceilings and an absolute monotonic `Instant` deadline. It supersedes `BorrowSpec.stdio`. The result contains only captured byte vectors and the ordinary exit/signal/leftover outcome, never a running child, pipe, fd or owning handle. Input and both captures progress concurrently with nonblocking parent pipe ends, so a child that ignores stdin cannot prevent deadline enforcement.

Unix uses the existing `run_borrowed` spawn door and explicit slot-3 mapping, environment annotation, git auto-gc/maintenance disabling, driver preparation and release rule. It introduces no additional containment backend or suspended-start barrier. Predecessor handling stays unchanged: Linux borrows declare no new predecessor record and clean up the borrowed child's process group and descendants; macOS uses the child's process group. Git Publication disables hooks in its own driver before calling this port, as Git spec §10 rule 4a requires.

Exceeding either byte ceiling returns `borrow-output-limit: stdout|stderr`; reaching the deadline returns `borrow-deadline: terminated|killed-after-grace` (`BorrowError::Deadline { termination }`). On either refusal, or an I/O failure (`borrow-io-failed`), SIGTERM is sent to the child group while the root remains unreaped; the handle's internal `terminate_grace_ms` field (beside `kill_wait_ms`, default 3000 ms, no new config key) bounds the grace. If the root exits during grace the deadline outcome is `terminated`; otherwise SIGKILL yields `killed-after-grace`. The root is then waited without reaping, the existing borrow domain's leftovers are ended, and the root is reaped before returning. The handle remains owned by the caller throughout. Remaining output is drained after normal root exit and leftover cleanup. As with `run_borrowed`, failure to end leftovers takes precedence and returns `borrow-leftover-not-killed`; this is never a successful empty-domain claim. Windows refuses this new form with `borrow-io-unsupported` before any child is started; its existing job-backed `run_borrowed` is unchanged.

2026-10-18: The Rust `validate(&Handle)` non-spawning entry and every `run_borrowed` family call validate the opaque acquired exclusive handle against the current lock resource using the existing file identity/borrower checks before spawning, refusing a replaced resource as `lock-resource-replaced` while keeping the descriptor private.

Clarified 2026-10-18 (refined): every acquire opens its own description. Outside a borrow, only the holder and its direct children between fork and exec can hold that description; it is close-on-exec everywhere else. On Linux drain, holders in the borrowed child's process group or descended from it are killed. A direct child outside the borrow group is protected as a pre-exec child while its locked copies retain `FD_CLOEXEC`: wait bounded by `killWaitMs` and re-check, never kill it. A tagged locked copy without `FD_CLOEXEC` proves explicit borrow mapping, so an adopted direct child with such a copy remains a borrower escapee and is killed. Unreadable descriptor flags never supply that authority. Any other holder of the description can only be an escaped descendant of a borrowed child, is inside the borrow's authority, and is killed, then drained and verified. Signals pin and re-check process identity. The Node fd facade routes drain through the door's `drainChild`, passing the held lock; the door excludes the calling process and applies this same rule. Unix borrowed children remain leaders of their own process groups. Non-spawning `validate_quiescent(&Handle)` has no borrow kill authority: it waits bounded and refuses unresolved holders before Publication writes Intent or supersession. A timeout or unprovable drain retains the held handle and exclusion; it never claims empty.

Clarified 2026-10-19: a narrowed per-spawn `Reach::Since` pass assumes that copies are inherited by fork, ordinary cyclic PID allocation is used (no privileged `clone3(set_tid)` or `ns_last_pid` override), and allocation stays below 4,000,000 PIDs/s inside the `pid_max / 4,000,000` window. An old or unreadable allocation mark falls back to start-time filtering over the process table. Descriptor transfers by `SCM_RIGHTS` or `pidfd_getfd` to pre-existing processes are outside that narrowed candidate set. The floor lags by one successful proof: proof N advances it only to the start of proof N-1, so a fork in flight at proof N remains eligible at N+1. Failed and out-of-order proofs do not advance it.

Clarified 2026-10-19 (supersedes the same-day full-scan admission/borrow-return rule): the narrowed `Reach::Since` pass is the only drain of a borrow return and of non-spawning `validate_quiescent`; it kills fork-inherited escapees promptly and never decides that the lock is free. The lock-freeing decision is made once, at exclusive Linux release. Capture the original description's stat key, exact fdinfo `major:minor:inode` token and the holder's proc-mount pid; reject a mismatched PID namespace. Open an independent, noncreating description through `/proc/self/fd/<fd>` and verify its inode before closing the original, so an unlinked/replaced pathname cannot redirect the later probe. This is an open, never a dup: the independent description is initially unlocked and does not retain the original flock.

After close, `/proc/locks` is read to EOF on one open seq_file and supplies positive evidence: a FLOCK record with the exact token and this process as locker proves a leaked copy. **An absent record does not prove release.** Kernel `seq_read_iter` can return a short page even into a larger userspace buffer, so the reader continues until EOF. This read is not an atomic snapshot and concurrent lock changes may affect it. With no matching record, try `LOCK_SH | LOCK_NB` on the independent inode-checked description: success proves the old EX description gone; close the probe immediately and return released. This brief SH hold can cause a concurrent exclusive `Wait::Try` acquirer to report held. The coordinator accepted this contention window after the short-read reproduction on 2026-10-19. Update, 2026-10-24: release tries the private `LOCK_SH | LOCK_NB` probe first, and a granted probe returns released; on refusal it enters the tagged descriptor scan over fdinfo. `/proc/locks` is not read at release.

A positive tagged record, blocked probe or any uncertainty enters the full tagged descriptor scan. Holders of this inode whose FLOCK record stamps this process are signalled by an identity captured before scanning their descriptors and pinned again at signal time, except direct pre-exec children whose locked copies retain `FD_CLOEXEC` (waited, never killed); a tagged non-CLOEXEC copy identifies an adopted borrower and is settled through this same door. A live own handle, or a positive record of a later acquirer, proves the old EX description gone by exclusivity and spares that acquirer and its borrowers. Recheck own handles before each signal; no kcmp is necessary once the own-handle proof holds. An empty scan alone does not prove release across an in-flight fork: repeat probe/scan until positively proven or `killWaitMs` passes, returning `lock-release-stuck` with killed count and remaining pids. Registry","sectionText":"## 7. Registry

[`packages/holder-lock/contracts/lock-registry.v1.json`](../../../packages/holder-lock/contracts/lock-registry.v1.json) (schema [`lock-registry.schema.v1.json`](../../../packages/holder-lock/contracts/lock-registry.schema.v1.json)) is the only list of which locks exist, in which order they may be taken. Rust and Node read the same file; the Node facade resolves the path templates (`<fgosDir>`, `<lockRoot>`, `<runDir>`, `<workflowRunDir>`).

`<eventOpenRoot>` is the resolved Git common directory plus `fgos/events`; Event Store owns its two repo mutexes, `event-seal` (58) and `event-append` (70), at `<eventOpenRoot>/locks/<name>.lock`. Both have no legacy path. Only Rust resolves this template; Node refuses these rows with `lock-not-node-owned`. Append is released before Git calls; seal is never taken inside the Work gate.

One row per lock: `name`, `kind`, `scope` (`repo`, `machine`, `run`), `rank`, `v3Path`, `owner` (the track that cut it over: `4.2`, `4.3`, `4.4`, `6.2`, `event-store`, `documentation`), and a note. The legacy path and shape and the fence of each row were deleted with the Node fence mechanism (section 12).

Ranks (a scope may only take a lock of a higher rank than every lock it holds):

| Rank | Locks | Kind |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | `runner`, `gateway`, `documentation-cutover` | lease |
| 15 | `attempt` | lease |
| 20 | `merge-slot` | mutex |
| 30 | `dispatch-cwd` | lease |
| 40 | `worktree-admin` | mutex |
| 50 | `main-checkout` | mutex |
| 55 | git's own `index.lock`: outside fgOS, no row; the hook tries rank 50 once | — |
| 58 | `event-seal` | mutex |
| 60 | `state`, `porting-events` | hot-mutex |
| 70 | `event-append` | mutex |
| 80 | leaves: `sessions`, `advance`, `reconcile`, `recovery`, `full-suite`, `provider-account`, `provider-state`, `observe`, `activation`, `install`, `project-config`, `global-config` | mutex, lease |

The ranks 58 (`event-seal`) and 70 (`event-append`) above are declared by the signed [Event Store spec §4](../event-store/spec.md#4-layering-and-locks), D-ADR0055 (nhật ký sự kiện là changeset niêm phong trên ref mỗi máy); implementation has not started. They are planned additions to the shipped registry, which currently declares neither rank nor lock. They do not claim a registered kind, path or cutover. The design permits `state` (60) → `event-append` (70) and forbids seal/sync under `state`; registry and implementation must land together under the Event Store proof gates.

Locks cut over by this track: `gateway`, `runner`, `sessions`, `advance`, `reconcile`, `recovery`, `full-suite`, `provider-account`, `provider-state`, `dispatch-cwd`. Their new files live under `<fgosDir>/locks/` (repo scope), `<lockRoot>/` (machine scope) or a `locks/` directory inside the run (`<workflowRunDir>/locks/advance.lock`, `<runDir>/locks/recovery.lock`), so a run's new lock never lands on the tombstone of its legacy path. The dispatch cwd lock is keyed by the directory's identity after `realpath` (`<fgosDir>/locks/dispatch-cwd--<dev>-<ino>.lock`), so a worktree reached through a symlink is the same lock. The npm package and the staged legacy-node payload ship the registry file, because every lock of this track resolves through it. The dispatch cwd lock keeps the `fgosDir` scope; a machine-wide cwd lock is a separate item, opened only when two workspaces share one cwd for real.

Locks cut over by the Rust-callers track (registry owner `4.4`), all leaves of rank 80, all mutex (their legacy paths were fenced by a tombstone directory at the cutover, section 12):

| Lock | Scope | New path | Legacy path (becomes a tombstone directory) | Caller |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `activation` | repo | `<fgosDir>/locks/activation-v2.lock` | `.fgos/installation/activation.lock` and `.fgos/locks/activation.lock` | `fgctl` init, upgrade, repair |
| `install` | machine | `<lockRoot>/install.lock` (`<stateRoot>/locks/install.lock`) | `<stateRoot>/install.lock` | `fgctl` release store |
| `observe` | repo | `<fgosDir>/locks/observe.lock` | `.fgos/observe/.lock` | Observe store (`fgos metrics`, `fgos friction`) |

Git adds `repo-config`, a repo mutex at rank 80, `<fgosDir>/locks/repo-config.lock`, with no legacy path. It serializes the local fetch-mapping writer; Git's native `config.lock` also excludes ordinary Git config writers.

| Name | Kind | Scope | Rank | v3Path | Owner | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `documentation-cutover` | lease | repo | 10 | `<fgosDir>/locks/documentation-cutover.lock` | `documentation` | Public acquire API only; no private holder-lock route. |

For this row, `<fgosDir>` is always the main checkout's `.fgos`, including calls from linked worktrees. The kernel handle serializes transitions only. The committed sidecar carries the persistent freeze described in section 19.

The predecessor domain rule","sectionText":"## 8. The predecessor domain rule

Measured on Windows: a lock bound to a process is released the moment that process dies, while the job that kills its children does so asynchronously, so for a few milliseconds the lock reads free while a borrowed git may still be writing. Linux and macOS have no such gap on the borrow path (git itself holds a copy of the description), but the rule is part of the port from the first driver so no driver can be written without it ([contract](../../../packages/holder-lock/contracts/predecessor.v1.json)).

0. **Release rule (custody extension, 2026-10-18).** The holder clears only its own unchanged predecessor record with `clear_domain(handle)` after observing its domain empty, while still holding exclusion, then closes. Execution does this after the runner commit receipt and persisted handoff. An absent record means a recorded handoff or that no producer ran. An unknown launch or unproven domain leaves the record for successor admission. `clear_domain` never kills a domain. **Limitation (owner decision 2026-10-19):** for a best-effort domain kind (`linux-pgroup`, `macos-tree`) "observed empty" sees the process group or tree only, so a `setsid` or double-fork escapee is not seen and a recorded handoff over such a domain does not cover it; admission after a controller death still refuses these kinds. On supervised Linux the attempt gate is a subreaper and kills adopted escapees before the receipt, so the exposure is unconfined Linux and macOS. Revisit when containment drivers give those platforms a provable domain.

   **Borrow cleanup.** Cleanup covers the borrowed child's process group, descendants and escaped description holders under §5's refined 2026-10-18 rule. Only direct pre-exec children of the holder outside the borrow group are waited, never killed. Hook-enabled borrows (including checkpoint and merge commits) still kill setsid/double-fork escapees holding the description; ancestry loss does not spare an escapee. A holder releases only after `run_borrowed` has waited for the child, killed leftovers in its authority, drained and verified empty. A non-empty predecessor domain found after the next holder took the lock means the previous holder died abnormally. On Linux the holder's own release settles against the kernel lock table as §5 describes; the next holder's predecessor rule is unchanged.
1. A holder that will create a process domain while it holds the lock (a job for `run_borrowed` on Windows; the attempt's namespace or job) writes `<lockFile>.predecessor.json` right after acquire and before creating the domain, while it still holds the lock: `{v: 1, domainKind, domainId}`. `domainKind` is `linux-pgroup` (best-effort), `linux-gate` (the gate's process tuple; empty iff `judge(tuple) == dead`), `windows-job` (a named Job Object) or `macos-tree` (a tree root tuple; best-effort). The record is written through a temp file and a rename. A missing record means the holder handed off after proving empty, or created no domain.
2. The next holder, after it holds the kernel lock, reads the record and asks the driver whether the domain is empty. Empty, or unopenable but proven empty: proceed. Not empty: kill the whole domain at once; never wait for it to drain.
3. Then wait at most `killWaitMs` (fixed at 2000 ms, `DEFAULT_KILL_WAIT_MS`; there is no config key; measured a few ms) for the killed processes to be signaled; the wait bounds the whole admission, so the time the kill itself spends waiting for an empty domain comes out of the same 2000 ms. Domain empty: proceed. Deadline passed, or the kill was refused: release the kernel lock and return `held (predecessor-domain-not-empty)` naming the domain; doctor shows that domain.
4. When the caller restricts `resource.predecessorKinds` (Node acquire params, Rust `Resource.predecessor_kinds`), acquisition checks that policy **under the kernel lock before ordinary predecessor cleanup**. Execution permits only `linux-gate` and `windows-job` for custody successors; it refuses best-effort or unknown records as `custody-predecessor-unknown` and preserves the worktree. There is no unlocked admission precheck: a busy kernel lock returns `dispatch-in-flight` on every platform before record policy is evaluated.
5. A holder that proceeded and will create a domain itself overwrites the record before creating it. A record with `v != 1`, or an unreadable record, is never deleted or ignored: acquire returns `held (predecessor-domain-not-empty)` with the raw record.

Why kill at once rather than wait for the domain to drain: a drain only helps a holder that was allowed to leave processes running after release, and step 0 forbids that. The second Windows measurement showed every contender waiting the full 2000 ms before terminating; killing at once brings the crash path down to a few milliseconds (p50 5.9 ms, p95 6.9 ms over 50 runs). A holder that violates step 0 on purpose has its leftover killed by the next holder: that is the holder's defect, and `lock-borrow-vectors` catches the known vectors.

`linux-gate` is judged by `judge(gate) == dead` and ended by SIGKILL by identity. On Linux `run_borrowed` declares no predecessor record; it kills the borrowed child's process group, descendants and escaped description holders under §5's refined rule, each signaled by identity. Direct pre-exec children of the holder outside the borrow group are waited and re-checked, never killed. Domain cleanup fails with a named error `borrow-leftover-not-killed` and the pid when one survives the deadline. On macOS the leftovers are the child's process group. `macos-tree` stays contract only until the run supervisor's macOS containment lands. `windows-job` is implemented, as section 8.1 says."},{"unitKind":"unheaded-block","anchor":"unheaded-block-45","githubAnchor":"unheaded-block-45","stableAnchor":"unheaded-block-45","title":"Unheaded block 45","startLine":185,"endLine":185,"textDigest":"396c188f6749b4fe8bdfdb517d7ba1790e2e5131fc83eae0ec6e7ad4aac3b773","sample":"Measured on Windows: a lock bound to a process is released the moment that process dies, while the job that kills its children does so asynchronously, so for a few milliseconds the","identityFingerprint":"94ba0fc3e55598e464fd1f638fdfd751932349a67ae22d05bd2d4b8aef90b71d","ancestry":["Holder-lock Component Specification","8. Plan and decisions: [plan 4.4b](../../../plans/261017-1256-windows-lockfileex-driver-and-macos-handoff/plan.md). The owner-machine probe that fixed the empty rule: [probe report](../../../plans/reports/probe-261017-0710-windows-predecessor-all-owners-dead-race.md); the review that shaped the views and the Node helper: [red-team](../../../plans/reports/red-team-261017-1330-windows-lockfileex-driver-plan-review.md).

- **Why not a handle.** A child that inherits a `LockFileEx` handle does not hold the lock, and the lock is released when the locking process dies. So `run_borrowed` on Windows never lends the lock: the locking process keeps holding it and runs the child inside a job it creates (`Local\fgos-borrow-<lock>-<pid>-<creation>-<counter>`, `KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE`, no breakaway). The child gets `FGOS_LOCK_JOB=<lock name>:<job name>`. A hook accepts it as the borrower (`--borrowed-check`) only when the env names this lock and a job, the predecessor record names that job and a holder tuple, the hook process is in the job, and the recorded holder is in its ancestor chain with the lock still held.
- **Record shape.** `domainKind: windows-job`, `domainId = {job, sessionId, declaredAt, holder: {host, pid, startTime}, keeper: {host, pid, startTime} | null}`, `v` stays 1. `declaredAt` and `startTime` are decimal FILETIME strings; `keeper` is filled by rewriting the record right after the keeper's ack, before any member exists. A string `domainId` parses to nothing, so it stays fail closed.
- **What the child inherits.** `std::process::Command` always passes `bInheritHandles = TRUE`, so a holder written with it would hand every inheritable handle it owns to git, its hooks and the keeper. Both the borrowed child and the keeper are started by `fgos_process::platform::windows_spawn::spawn` instead: `CreateProcessW` with `STARTUPINFOEXW` and `PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_HANDLE_LIST`, so the child inherits the copies made for its three standard streams (a pipe, `NUL`, a file or the caller's own stream) and nothing else; with no stream handle at all, `bInheritHandles` is `FALSE`. A batch file as the borrowed program is refused (`cmd.exe` quoting is not something this driver takes on); no borrowed command is one.
- **Two views of the domain.** The **job view** (release rule and keeper): `ActiveProcesses == 0` and every member named by the job's pid list or by a Toolhelp scan for `IsProcessInJob` is signaled. The **contender view** (`admit`, after the kernel lock is held): a live recorded holder released normally, so the job view decides and only `TerminateJobObject` ever runs; a dead holder gives the union of the job list, the in-job scan and the holder's descendants created at or after `declaredAt` (minus the keeper), re-read on every poll. A pid that is live but cannot be opened keeps the domain not empty. A job that does not open falls back to the tree source with two consecutive quiet snapshots. In that fallback, a process created at or after `declaredAt` whose parent has left the snapshot (or whose pid now belongs to a newer process), and its descendants, are also waited for, for 200 ms after the job was first found gone (a one-shot window; nothing new is named after it closes): a member of a closed job whose parent already exited is no longer reachable from the holder and is still tearing down (measured on Windows CI: a live git pid named by no source, one in about 150 rounds). A holder pid that now belongs to a newer process ends the clause (the holder died a while ago, nothing is tearing down). The 200 ms window is a timing assumption: a member whose teardown outlasts it and that no other source names could still slip, and the owner's 500-repeat gate is the test for it. They are only waited for, never signaled, because an unrelated orphan looks the same. A record of another session is `NotEmpty` with reason `predecessor-other-session`. The contract is [`predecessor.v1.json`](../../../packages/holder-lock/contracts/predecessor.v1.json) `windowsJobViews`.
- **Keeper.** The locking process spawns `job-keeper` before the job has a member and keeps it outside the job. It exits only when the holder has said `finished` (or its handle is signaled) and the job view is empty, polling every 50 ms with the list and count only. A crash during a borrowed git commit therefore costs about 120-170 ms at the next acquire.
- **`lock-hold` route.** Node cannot call `LockFileEx`, so on Windows it starts one `fgos internal lock-hold` helper per held lock ([contract](../../../packages/holder-lock/contracts/internal-route.lock-hold.v1.json)). Node and the helper talk through files in a private work directory (`ready.json`, `req-<n>.json`, `started-<n>.json`, `result-<n>.json`, output logs), never stdin, because libuv queues pipe writes until the loop turns and `Atomics.wait` blocks the loop. Release is `TerminateProcess` of the helper plus a bounded wait. Parent death during a borrow ends the job at once.
- **Helper roles.** The crate API takes `HelperExe`. Production passes the running executable; tests pass `env!("CARGO_BIN_EXE_...")`. Roles (`probe-holder`, `job-keeper`) are entered as `fgos internal holder-lock-helper <role>` and as the hidden `fgctl internal holder-lock-helper <role>`, so the `fgctl` gate never runs anything under the candidate release.
- **Windows borrow-vector assertion.** The four vector names and the sibling check are the same. Each background command writes its Windows pid; the vector opens its own `SYNCHRONIZE` handle to it and asserts the handle is signaled when `run_borrowed` returns. The check does not use the driver's own empty rule, and it does not rely on `probe == Free`, which is trivially true on Windows.
- **Doctor.** `lock-holders` judges a `windows-job` record with the read-only `fgos internal lock-fd --predecessor-state <lockFile>` (one contender-view pass, never kills): `empty` and `absent` are fine, `not-empty` and `unknown` warn with the domain and the reason (for example `predecessor-other-session`). `linux-gate` and `macos-tree` records keep the Node `judge()` path.
- **macOS unchanged.** The `flock` driver and the activation gate are as before; `macos-tree` containment is not part of this work.
- **Quiesce scan on Windows.** The scan stays unsupported there (Toolhelp has no command line), so `fgos events migrate` asks a person to attest that every process is stopped.
- **CI and gate.** `.github/workflows/holder-lock-cross-platform.yml` runs the Rust and Node tests on `windows-latest` and `macos-latest`. The acceptance gate is the 500-repeat predecessor stress run on the owner's machine (`apps/fgos/tests/windows_predecessor_stress.rs`).

Async fd borrows may overlap, but their successful returns are not independent: a completed borrow waits for protected siblings up to `killWaitMs` and fails closed if any remain. The private owning handle records live sibling borrow roots and passes them both to the existing async drain (`--protected-roots`) and into native loans; Rust drains protect their process groups and descendants from signals. A drain snapshot refuses starting another async/synchronous borrow or minting a native loan with retryable `borrow-drain-in-progress`, before spawn. This bounded refusal is contention, not an authority failure. After the sweep returns, a caller may retry admission. A native Git call overlapping a live async sibling can likewise fail closed at drain without killing that sibling or retrying a Git effect. Node facade and `LockScope`","sectionText":"## 9. Node facade and `LockScope`

`src/holder-lock/` is the Node facade. A caller never sees an fd. On Linux and macOS every lock operation runs in the caller's process through the `holderLock` namespace of the combined addon of the activated release whose payload is running; the facade's `driver.mjs` is the only module that touches it. There is no lock implemented in Node: without the addon every acquire fails `lock-driver-unavailable` with reason `addon-not-shipped` (naming `npm run fgos:dev`), `addon-unavailable` or `no-host-binary`.

The door is a capability. `holderLock.take()` hands one registration per worker thread to the facade's `driver.mjs`; `lockFd`, `drainChild`, `releaseFd`, `clearDomain` and `closeHandedOver` need it, so possession of a path, an fd number or request data never grants authority. Code that loads the addon before the facade can consume the capability and deny facade startup (fail closed); a hostile module or worker thread needs process isolation, not this guard. `lockFd` returns a typed External that owns a duplicate of the description and the creation marks; the facade keeps it beside its own fd in a private WeakMap and never exports it. `LockHandle` construction requires acquisition's private token, and `release()` refuses while the synchronous bridge borrows the handle. The Rust admission method is unsafe because its caller must prove acquired-description provenance (§19). Windows native handover refuses with `git-lock-handover-unsupported`; the helper-owned transport is not exported as a descriptor.

- `acquireSync(scope, name, params, {waitMs})` and `acquire(...)` (async: the door's try repeated on a timer, so the runner loop does not poll in a child). The facade opens the lock file `O_RDWR | O_CREAT`, calls `lockFd`, and checks the inode after acquire. The predecessor kill wait is the fixed `DEFAULT_KILL_WAIT_MS` (2000 ms); there is no config key.
- **Bounded blocking.** In process, a dead predecessor's kill wait inside `lockFd` and a borrow drain inside `drainChild` block the event loop for at most `DEFAULT_KILL_WAIT_MS` (2 s), on the contended path only (a dead holder's domain must be killed first). Before the door the same wait ran in a helper child while the async `acquire` polled. The bound is accepted; a libuv thread for the admission would be an addition for a rare path.
- `handle.release()` commits the handle's state (descriptor closed, `released`, untracked from its scope) and then settles against the kernel lock table, returning `{ settled: 'released' | 'stuck' | 'closed', killed, pids }` as the Rust port does. It never throws for a stuck settle, because it runs in `finally` blocks everywhere and a throw would replace the caller's result; escaped copies of a `stuck` settle are left for `lock-holders` and `fgos lock fence` to show. A handle handed over to a borrowed child is closed without settling. It never calls `LOCK_UN`.
- `probe(name, params)` is the door's `probe`: a fresh description, one shared try, closed at once.
- `runBorrowed(handle, spec, {sync | async})` is the only function that puts the lock fd into `stdio`; it sets `FGOS_LOCK_FD=<name>:3` and, for git, prepends the gc flags. The async form returns the child for a caller that needs `onSpawn` (the account lock).
- `lockHolders` returns the processes holding a lock file as tuples with the `origin` Rust decided (`foreign`, `borrowed`, `host-payload`, `attempt-member`), so no caller classifies a holder from a command line.
- `held` with reason `predecessor-domain-not-empty` becomes the named error `lock-predecessor-domain-not-empty` with the domain; `borrow-leftover-not-killed` keeps its name.
- The host binary is still needed for the processes that remain (`lock-fd --borrowed-check` and `--shared-try` for the git hook, the Windows `lock-hold` helper); it is found once per process by `resolveActiveHostBin` (`FGOS_HOST_BIN`, then the activation), the same rule Session Identity uses, and exec'd directly, never through a shim.

`LockScope` is an object passed explicitly through calls; every parallel `claimAndDispatch` in the runner has its own. Inside one scope a lock may be acquired only at a rank higher than every rank the scope holds; two locks of the same rank in one scope are forbidden. A violation throws `lock-order-violation` with `{held, acquiring}` at once. There is no trace-then-warn release and no environment switch: the full test suite and dogfood expose a wrong order, and the phase that caused it fixes it. Exclusion between two scopes of one process is the kernel's job (two descriptions), so no process-wide rank set exists. Across processes (hook, helper) no order check is needed: the hook tries once and never waits, the helper holds nothing after it exits."},{"unitKind":"unheaded-block","anchor":"unheaded-block-53","githubAnchor":"unheaded-block-53","stableAnchor":"unheaded-block-53","title":"Unheaded block 53","startLine":221,"endLine":221,"textDigest":"45b06af90feabc1f2575cc59ce18513281ac210a6bbc58e0289c360d09112f8d","sample":"`src/holder-lock/` is the Node facade. The routes live in `apps/fgos/src/main.rs` as the earliest branch of `main()` (before any composition, provider or spawn, so no child can inherit fd 3). They are not in `command-routes.json` and not in help. Every lock route (`lock-fd`, `lock-hold`, `lock-borrow-vectors`) requires `--protocol 2` and answers `v` and `protocol` 2; absent or different, the answer is `host-version-mismatch` (one release, one protocol). `quiesce-scan` is the one exception and stays on protocol 1. Each prints one JSON line on stdout (`{v, protocol, ...}`, both 2 for a lock route and both 1 for `quiesce-scan`); stderr is for people and never parsed.

2026-10-20 (phase 07 unit 22, owner decision): route protocol 2. The lock routes moved from protocol 1 to 2 so that a stale global npm `fgos merge` (an old Node payload that sends `--protocol 1`) is refused by the new host with `host-version-mismatch`, which the facade surfaces as `unavailable/host-version-mismatch`, and an old Node facade that talks to a new host fails closed because every answer carries protocol 2 (its parser accepts only 1). Only the current protocol is accepted: there is no dual-accept window, because the mismatch is the point. The lock routes share the one constant (`PROTOCOL` in `src/holder-lock/protocol.mjs`, `route.rs`) and bump together. `quiesce-scan` keeps its own protocol 1 (`SCAN_PROTOCOL`): it is read-only, its contract does not tie it to the lock protocol, and its other callers (`fgctl` activation, the distribution git gate) pin it themselves.

2026-10-21 (owner decision, option 1): `quiesce-scan` stays on protocol 1 so an old payload can still run its quiescence check before it is upgraded. Caveat: the host scans linked worktrees only from the caller's repeated `--dir`, and a Node payload older than Git 07 sends none, so a new host paired with an old payload (only possible on a compatibility channel, for example global npm `fgos` with a newer `FGOS_HOST_BIN`; `fgctl` always stages host and payload of one release) scans the workspace root only and can miss a process working in a linked worktree. If such a mixed pair is ever seen, the follow-up is that the host refuses a scan without `--dir` unless `--workspace-only` is passed.

`stateRoot` is resolved by one function in the crate, the same formula `resolve_machine_release_store_root` uses, so the release store and the locks never disagree ([vectors](../../../packages/holder-lock/contracts/state-root.vectors.v1.json)):

1. `FGOS_STATE_ROOT` (`pinned`): used verbatim.
2. `FGOS_STATE_HOME` (`fgos-state-home`): used verbatim, no suffix.
3. `XDG_STATE_HOME/fgos` (`xdg-state-home`).
4. `HOME/.local/state/fgos` (`home`); `USERPROFILE/.local/state/fgos` only when `HOME` is unset.
5. `.local/state/fgos` relative (`relative-fallback`).

A variable whose value is blank is unset; a non-blank value is used untrimmed. `lockRoot` is `<stateRoot>/locks`. The Rust host resolves the root once and exports `FGOS_STATE_ROOT` before it execs the Node payload; Node reads that variable. Where it is absent (a payload the host did not start, such as a test process) `resolveStateRoot` asks the door (`holderLock.stateRoot(env)`, the host's own formula) and never guesses; with no addon it fails `lock-driver-unavailable`, naming the dev door. The checkout channel (`node bin/fgos.mjs`) is unsupported for the lock verbs: run through `fgos` or `npm run fgos:dev -- <verb>`. Dispatch pins `FGOS_STATE_ROOT` into the environment of every child, so a sandbox with its own `HOME` does not move the root; a process that sets another root is, by definition, another machine scope. The key of a cwd is `dev:ino` after `realpath`."},{"unitKind":"unheaded-block","anchor":"unheaded-block-61","githubAnchor":"unheaded-block-61","stableAnchor":"unheaded-block-61","title":"Unheaded block 61","startLine":253,"endLine":253,"textDigest":"8efc23f8d9c4502666400436eb2fcdc418b01a23bb8d9be38be8e78035c39e47","sample":"`stateRoot` is resolved by one function in the crate, the same formula `resolve_machine_release_store_root` uses, so the release store and the locks never disagree ([vectors](../..","identityFingerprint":"79b70a2ca2a615326ef189a6e5b17bdc3d999f8fa866a9bc9ff159f61c7f7e13","ancestry":["Holder-lock Component Specification","11. Cutover history","sectionText":"## 12. Cutover history

The locks of this track moved to their kernel-lock paths in a stop-everything cutover (2026-10-17): every writer in every workspace was stopped, each lock moved to its new path and the legacy path was deleted in the same phase, with no family marker and no protocol floor. Each retired path was fenced once so an older binary failed loudly (`EISDIR`, or "held by pid 1" for the provider ledgers) rather than holding a legacy lock beside a kernel lock: tombstone directories for the fixed paths, per-run, per-cwd, `main-checkout`, `merge-slot`, `state` and `porting-events`, `activation`, `install` and `observe`, and a blocking generation for the provider ledgers. The Node mechanism that placed and checked them (`src/holder-lock/fences.mjs`, the doctor row `lock-fences` and its fix) was removed on 2026-10-22 under the one-release policy: no code reads a legacy lock path, and the tombstones already on disk stay as they are. Rollback to a pre-cutover release is by hand: remove the `TOMBSTONE` directories of exactly the registry paths, and publish one more generation with `releasedAt` on each blocked ledger. The WAL activation fence is Git's: `fgctl` places it inside its activation critical section, and the doctor row `git-operation-journal` reports `git-fence-missing` when it is absent. The stop-everything scan that `fgos events migrate` needs is `quiesce-scan` (section 10) with its caller in that verb."},{"unitKind":"unheaded-block","anchor":"unheaded-block-64","githubAnchor":"unheaded-block-64","stableAnchor":"unheaded-block-64","title":"Unheaded block 64","startLine":265,"endLine":265,"textDigest":"5700142fdae3a2eff60160b4c2e219d740723b954213898ee279a41062a6c142","sample":"The locks of this track moved to their kernel-lock paths in a stop-everything cutover (2026-10-17): every writer in every workspace was stopped, each lock moved to its new path and","identityFingerprint":"333cee60dbe3bd14089458d16937abc9a7ddd877e9979e8245aacfd2ad9cf7fc","ancestry":["Holder-lock Component Specification","12. `fgos setup` creates `<lockRoot>` and `<fgosDir>/locks` with mode 0700 when they are missing and tightens an existing one to 0700 (fix `lock-dirs`). It registers no config default: the predecessor kill wait is fixed (section 8), and an existing `lock` section in a config file is ignored.

`fgos doctor` checks, registered in `src/setup/registrations.mjs` with their bodies in `src/setup/holder-lock-checks.mjs`. Levels follow the doctor convention: `passed: false` fails, a message starting with `warning:` warns, `info:` is informational. Messages carry no timings, so two doctor runs over the same state print the same text:

| Check | Does | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `lock-kernel-semantics` | For `<fgosDir>/locks` and `<lockRoot>`: the door's guarantee plus a two-process probe on that same mount (a child holds EX, the parent must see `held`; the child dies, the parent must see `free`) | Prints `{driver, exclusion, borrow, holders}`, then `stateRoot <root> (<source>)` and `killWaitMs 2000 (fixed)`. `kernel` with a green probe passes (on Windows the probe runs over a `lock-hold` helper and the message shows `lockfileex`); a missing directory warns until setup creates it; a guarantee of `unsupported` (a platform with no driver), a network filesystem (`none`), an unresolved lock root or state root, and a door that cannot be reached fail by name |
| `lock-borrow-vectors` | `fgos internal lock-borrow-vectors` | Any red vector or a red sibling check fails; `unavailable` (no git) fails too, as activation refuses it. Runs on every platform, with the Windows assertion of section 8.1 |
| `lock-holders` | The kernel's holder list for every existing lock file of the registry rows (run and account rows enumerated from their directories), the predecessor records beside them, and the `state` and `porting-events` hot records | A holder warns with pid and cmdline when its `origin` is `foreign`. A `<lock>.predecessor.json` whose domain is not judged dead, whose version is unknown, or which names a Windows job the host does not judge empty warns with the domain and the reason; a record written in another PID namespace judges `unknown` and keeps warning until a person confirms the domain is gone and removes the record. A hot record that does not parse, is open by another process, or names a holder the judge answers `unknown` for more than five minutes warns with the file and `fgos lock fence <resource>`; a younger `unknown` is a busy holder and passes. Holders that cannot be listed are informational |
| `writer-identity-resolvable` | The writer identity through the activation's host | Fails when no host answers or the answer mismatches (session identity spec) |
| `convention-conformance` | Post-cutoff violations of the naming convention | Fails on a violation; passes otherwise (convention spec) |

The check `provider-capacity-lock-stale` is removed with its body: the provider-capacity ledger is no longer a mutex once the provider locks are kernel locks.

`fgctl` gates activation: right before it publishes the activation file on every path (init, upgrade, repair) it runs, through the crate it links itself and never under the candidate directory, the guarantee plus the two-process semantics probe for `<workspace>/.fgos/locks` and `<lockRoot>`, and the borrow vectors. On Linux and macOS a red probe or vector refuses the activation with `lock-kernel-semantics-failed` or `lock-borrow-vectors-failed` and the detail. The gate runs on Windows too, with the `fgctl` binary as its own helper; a platform whose driver reports itself unsupported refuses with `lock-kernel-semantics-failed` (`no holder-lock driver on <platform>`). A network filesystem is refused by name. There is no flag that turns the gate off. The main checkout is written by claim, merge, land and the `.fgos` checkpoint. Its single guard is the `main-checkout` mutex (rank 50, `<fgosDir>/locks/main-checkout.lock`, [registry](../../../packages/holder-lock/contracts/lock-registry.v1.json)): a kernel lock like every other mutex, so it has no TTL, no ambiguous state, no recognition of a holder by pid and no protocol marker. The kernel answers `held` or `free`; nothing in the component decides anything from a pid or a clock.

**One door.** Code reaches the main checkout through `withMainCheckout(scope, purpose, fn)`, which acquires the mutex in the caller's `LockScope` (section 9) and hands `fn` a `mainHandle`. A function that must write under the lock (the `.fgos` checkpoint) takes the handle as a required argument and never acquires by itself. A caller that already holds main (claim) passes its handle down; a merge holds only its slot while it merges and verifies in a temporary worktree, and calls `withMainCheckout` just for the checkpoint, the merge commit and the land. The order in a scope is fixed by rank: merge slot 20, `worktree-admin` 40, main checkout 50 (the state store locks sit at 60 in the registry).

**The merge slot** is a mutex per target ref (rank 20), at `<fgosDir>/locks/merge-slot--<encodeURIComponent(ref)>.lock`; the encoded ref is what v1 already wrote. It serialises merges into one ref and is released after the merge, after main.

**Borrowing replaces `FGOS_MAIN_LOCK_HOLDER_PID`.** The holder runs every git child of a checkpoint or merge through `runBorrowed` (section 3), which gives the locked description to exactly that child in slot 3 with `FGOS_LOCK_FD=main-checkout:3` and prepends `-c gc.auto=0 -c maintenance.auto=false` ([contract](../../../packages/holder-lock/contracts/main-checkout-borrow.v1.json)). The `.githooks/pre-commit` hook, which git runs inside that child, is a borrower only when the three conditions of section 5 hold, checked by `fgos internal lock-fd --protocol 2 --borrowed-check <lock path>`. A borrower skips the activity beacon, because the lock proves who is committing. Anything else is a stranger: the hook probes `main-checkout` once with a description of its own, refuses when it is held, and never waits (git already holds `index.lock`, rank 55). The child cannot release the lock for the holder, cannot pass the description on beyond git's own hooks and cannot start anything in the background; the holder waits for the child before the transaction counts as done. The worker base env of a dispatch drops `FGOS_LOCK_FD`; a leaked variable gives nothing without the description.

`FGOS_MAIN_LOCK_HOLDER_PID`, the holder record with its `ttlMs`, the recognition of the same identity as a refresh, the `protocol.json` marker and the `ambiguous` state of v1 do not exist in v3. A stuck holder is handled by section 17."},{"unitKind":"unheaded-block","anchor":"unheaded-block-70","githubAnchor":"unheaded-block-70","stableAnchor":"unheaded-block-70","title":"Unheaded block 70","startLine":287,"endLine":287,"textDigest":"738396745a4eda78cfedfedae87dad20a7c480e7c110818e46e8cb7c05d2aae2","sample":"The main checkout is written by claim, merge, land and the `.fgos` checkpoint. Hot state mutex and porting events","sectionText":"## 15. Hot state mutex and porting events

The state store takes one transaction at a time per clone through `withStateTx(fgosDir, fn, {resource})` ([`src/state/hot-lock.mjs`](../../../src/state/hot-lock.mjs), contract [`hot-lock.v1.json`](../../../packages/holder-lock/contracts/hot-lock.v1.json)). `resource` is `state` (work events, claims, the state view) or `porting-events` (the porting log); both are registry rows of rank 60, kind `hot-mutex`. The mutex replaces `events.lock`, `runtime/claims.lock` and `porting/events.lock`: claims and events are one critical section, so the worker-slot ceiling is checked in the same transaction as the claim. Code that must reach a hot resource gets the transaction object `tx` (`append`, `writeJson`, `writeText`, `rename`, `readJson`, `unlink`; paths confined to the `.fgos`), which is revoked when the callback returns.

**Fast path and record.** Acquire is `link()` of a whole temp file onto `<fgosDir>/locks/<resource>.hot`; release is `unlink`. The record is `{v, pid, startTime, bootId, pidNs, writer}`. A live holder is never taken over. Wait is 5 s, polling every 10 ms, then `hot-lock-timeout`.

**Cleanup of a dead holder** happens only under the kernel lock `<resource>.reclaim.lock` (the registry row's `v3Path`, taken through this facade): the judge of the whole tuple answers `dead` (a zombie counts as dead), the record is read again and its bytes equal what the judge saw, and only then is it unlinked. A record that does not parse, or whose judge answers `unknown` (no readable process table, a foreign pid namespace, a record of another host), is never cleaned: the waiter times out with reason `lock-record-unreadable`, the `lock-holders` doctor check names the file, and a person who confirmed the holder is gone runs `fgos lock fence state` (section 17). The record is the process door's own tuple of the writer (`selfRecord`), on Windows too (the creation time, FILETIME, decimal, in `startTime`); the judge reads the same door for a recorded pid, with no spawn and no cache. The verdicts are the table of the Rust judge: absent or exited is `dead`, the recorded creation time is `alive`, another creation time is a reused pid and `dead`, an unopenable process or a record of another host is `unknown` and fails closed. The doctor check and `fgos lock fence` read the record through the same judge (`judgeHotRecord`).

**Release limit.** The hot lock is released by unlinking its record. When that unlink stays blocked (a Windows writer whose record another process keeps open) `releaseRecord` throws `hot-lock-release-stuck` after a short bound. `withStateTx` releases in a `finally`, so that error replaces the callback's own error or result; the known consequence is that a caller sees the release failure and not the error of its transaction. It only reaches a Windows writer whose unlink stayed blocked for 25 ms.

**Critical section rules, thrown at once.** The callback is synchronous; a thenable result throws `state-tx-async`. Starting a child process inside the section (any `child_process` export, including named ESM imports) throws `exec-under-hot-lock` at the call; acquiring a hot mutex again in the same process throws `hot-lock-reentry` without waiting. Values that need git or the host (`mainFgosDir`, `head`, the writer identity) are read before the lock and passed in as `prefetched`. There is no switch that turns the guard off.

**Lock order.** Hot mutexes sit at rank 60, above the main checkout (50): a claim reads HEAD, takes the `state` transaction for the check and the claim record, and takes main only around the `.fgos` checkpoint, never inside the state transaction.

Nothing in the repo-lock core (sections 14, 16) imports the event log, a shard or `withStateTx`; the `.fgos` checkpoint of the main door stays a detachable adapter. `worktree-admin` is a mutex (rank 40, `<fgosDir>/locks/worktree-admin.lock`) with no v1 predecessor and no fence. It wraps every fgOS call of `git worktree add`, `git worktree remove`, `git worktree move` (relocate) and `git worktree prune`. For remove and relocate, the dirty-check of the worktree, the destroy or move, and the registration change run under one hold of the lock, so no other worktree administration can run between the check and the effect (Git lessons G-042, G-155). It stays one lock: there is no second admin lock, and read-only listing takes none. Rank 40 is below main checkout (50), so no wrapped worktree command runs while main is held: a claim creates its worktree after it has released main; a merge creates its temporary worktree under the merge slot (20), before it takes main.

Amended 2026-10-17 by owner decision (Git G0 Q6); implemented by the Rust Git Worktree port in phase 03 (2026-10-19), including operation-specific prune/repair under the same rank-40 scope. The public create verb uses this door; runner, session and integration callers move onto the Worktree port in Git phase 07. Status: implemented in the port; complete once the one-door gate (`git-mutation-one-door`, Git spec §12) reports zero undeclared worktree writers (on 2026-10-20 one raw `git worktree remove --force` remained in `bin/fgos.mjs`, owned by the last phase 07 unit). Before this amendment the lock wrapped `git worktree add` only, and `remove` and `prune` stayed unwrapped because they had no recorded incident. The Git component spec ([docs/platform/git/spec.md](../git/spec.md) §5) states which Git operations take this lock and which locks a caller may already hold."},{"unitKind":"unheaded-block","anchor":"unheaded-block-82","githubAnchor":"unheaded-block-82","stableAnchor":"unheaded-block-82","title":"Unheaded block 82","startLine":315,"endLine":315,"textDigest":"e682f99aa53fadc7c08ee4baf38da4ec783325588b397031ee70885af863b3f8","sample":"`worktree-admin` is a mutex (rank 40, `<fgosDir>/locks/worktree-admin.lock`) with no v1 predecessor and no fence. A hung live holder is never taken over. `fgos lock fence <name>` is the one door a person uses for it, and it replaces `unlock --force`:

1. It lists every process that holds a description of the lock file (Linux: the door's `holders`) and shows each with pid and cmdline.
2. It asks the person to confirm.
3. It sends SIGTERM and then SIGKILL to each by identity ([process spec](../process/spec.md)); the lock releases when they are dead. There is no path that takes a lock from a live holder.
4. Where holders are `unlistable` (macOS, Windows) the person stops the process and runs `fgos lock fence <name> --attest-stopped`, which only re-checks by try-lock.
5. A hot mutex (`state`, `porting-events`, section 15) is held by its record file, not by a kernel lock the holder keeps. `fgos lock fence state` reads the record: a holder it proves alive is ended like any other holder (after confirmation); a record that does not parse, or whose holder cannot be judged here (a process the Windows host cannot open, a foreign pid namespace), is removed only with `--attest-stopped`. Known limits","sectionText":"## 19. Known limits

- Git Worktree remove/move cannot acquire rank 30 while holding rank 40. It rechecks custody and live cwd immediately before TargetAttempt and again before the Git call, but a new rank-30 acquirer can still race the final probe. Cross-user unreadable cwd and privileged actors are outside its same-user process guarantee; shared cross-user checkout custody is not certified.

- A live holder that is wedged keeps its lock until it exits: a dispatcher stuck on a cwd blocks that cwd with no time limit (the legacy lock had a 4-hour ttl and a reconcile clear; `dispatch reconcile clear-cwd-lock` now only reports held or free). The worker it started is still killed at its run timeout.
- A hung live holder is never taken over. A person fences it (section 17); the lock releases when it dies.
- `holders()` is `unlistable` on macOS and Windows, so `lock-holders` and the leftover kill of `run_borrowed` rely on the process group there (best-effort).
- The supervisor declares its attempt domain on the cwd lease on every platform. A best-effort `linux-pgroup` or `macos-tree` record cannot prove successor custody after controller death; Execution refuses that worktree even when the group appears empty. A crash while a borrow runs on Windows costs the next acquire about 120-170 ms.
- The dispatch cwd lock keeps the `fgosDir` scope: two workspaces whose `.fgos` directories differ do not exclude each other on one cwd.
- A borrower hook's `LOCK_EX | LOCK_NB` on an inherited description also succeeds when nobody holds the lock; that only happens when the API hands over a description it has not locked, which is a programming error, since the API only passes a description after acquire.
- Execution retains one dispatch-cwd lease across a Unit run, provider failover, runner commit, receipt and handoff. Commit git/hook children and the Unit verify command borrow it. Unknown launch/recovery failures release the controller copy without clearing its predecessor. Workflow preserves the refused checkout and branch and redispatches once into a fresh worktree from the recorded base; explicit `fgos run --worktree` stops with the typed cause.
- `FGOS_HOST_BIN` is inherited, so a child uses its parent's host binary; a release whose route speaks another protocol answers `host-version-mismatch` and the facade fails closed.
- A copy-holder that changes the lock type on the shared description (`LOCK_SH` on an exclusive copy) re-stamps the record with its own pid and briefly drops the lock; it is then indistinguishable from a later acquirer, is not killed, and shows in `lock-holders` as a non-fgOS holder until it exits."},{"unitKind":"unheaded-block","anchor":"unheaded-block-87","githubAnchor":"unheaded-block-87","stableAnchor":"unheaded-block-87","title":"Unheaded block 87","startLine":335,"endLine":335,"textDigest":"3eb22a047cede4931d5c5d5cabd0041b23de5468f877675f3e6633305c0afe54","sample":"- Git Worktree remove/move cannot acquire rank 30 while holding rank 40. Existing symlink spellings still share one key. This changes the key: use the phase's stop-everything cutover; old and new controllers must never coexist.

To recover that same checkout manually: stop all dispatchers for it, identify the exact lock path in the refusal, inspect its `.predecessor.json` (`fgos doctor` prints it with the host's judgement in `lock-holders`), fence the recorded producer and every possible descendant (including escaped sessions), and verify no writer remains. Known limits"],"text":"### Documentation-cutover write lease","sectionText":"### Documentation-cutover write lease

The lease freezes documentation writes across processes without a TTL. Its authority is the committed `plans/documentation-cutover-lease.json` blob on `refs/heads/main`. Working-tree copies are not authority. A held sidecar keeps refusing non-holders after process death or loss of the kernel lock resource.

| Command | Result |
|---|---|
| `fgos docs-lease acquire [--worktree <path>]` | Select a registered holder checkout in this repository, create its random token, record main's base commit and scope digests, and commit the held sidecar. Without `--worktree`, use the caller's checkout root. A held lease refuses another acquire, including by its holder. |
| `fgos docs-lease status [--json]` | Report state and, while held, age, holder worktree, token hash, scope digests and kernel-lock probe. Corrupt authority is reported as held/corrupt. |
| `fgos docs-lease release` | Authenticate the caller checkout's token, commit released state with `releaseScopeDigests` and `drift`, then remove that checkout's token. Drift is reported and does not prevent release. |
| `fgos docs-lease abandon --owner-confirmed --reason "<reason>"` | Commit owner-confirmed abandoned state with a non-empty written reason. This is the only repair door for a corrupt committed sidecar. Token possession is not required. |

Each successful transition makes one sidecar-only ScopedCommit in main. It takes `documentation-cutover` (10), then `main-checkout` (50), in one LockScope, and releases both handles afterwards. Busy transition/main locks refuse. Main must be checked out on `refs/heads/main`; a moved baseline refuses as `base-moved` without an internal retry. Acquire validates repository membership, rejects a holder nested inside frozen scope, and records tree/blob OIDs at the pinned main baseline, including explicit absent roots. It does not run the cutover's worktree-cleanliness, unmerged-branch, inventory or rehearsal checks; the cutover operator owns those checks. If acquisition publishes held state but receipt validation fails, cleanup keeps the token when committed main still names its hash or committed evidence is corrupt/unreadable, preserving recovery access.

The fixed scope is:

- `docs/**`, including `docs/transitional-switchboard.md`;
- root `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md`;
- the [switchboard JSON](../../../plans/260925-documentation-authority-unification/transitional-switchboard.json);
- `core/skills/**`, `.agents/skills/**` and `plugins/fgOS/skills/**`;
- `plans/documentation-cutover-lease.json` itself.

Other plan evidence and code/test roots are outside the freeze. The sidecar is transition evidence and is excluded from its own scope digest.

Pre-commit refuses scoped non-holder commits in every worktree. Raw moves of main into frozen scope refuse even for holders; the [Git hook contract](../git/spec.md#7-hardened-git-backend-parsers-and-hook-contract) defines the sidecar-transition exception.

Production admission doors explicitly declare the caller checkout; holder identity is never inferred from ambient cwd. The shared `leaseAdmission` gate always reads authority from the gated `repoRoot` repository's `refs/heads/main`. While held, the declared caller must resolve to the same main checkout as that repository before its token or a code-only footprint can admit it. Foreign-repository and non-Git callers are refused, including for read-only work; a copied foreign token or a foreign repository's free sidecar cannot authorize them. The low-level gate falls back to `process.cwd()` only when no `repoRoot` is supplied; every production door supplies one. The execution door's non-repository read-only exception applies only when the gated root itself is outside Git.

| Admission door | Caller and effect boundary |
|---|---|
| Unit execution (`runUnit`) | Declared caller checkout; refuses all non-holder work, including read-only Units, before execution effects. |
| Workflow start | Declared origin checkout; admits before config, ledger, advance, spawn or generated worktree effects, and records origin in `case.opened.payload.callerCheckout`. |
| Workflow resume/answer | Recorded origin decides admission before advance, answer writes or spawn. An answer from another checkout of the same repository is admitted for a holder-origin Workflow; the answerer's checkout does not replace its origin. Generated writer checkouts never become holder identity. |
| Runner Land (`landRunnerItem`) | Explicit caller checkout, separately from destination/main; checks before checkpoint or Land effects. |
| Workflow Land (`mergeWorkflowBranch`) | Recorded Workflow origin passed as caller; checks before native Land, including for an already-integrated branch. |

Admission is reused only within its operation; detached children refresh it, and each Land checks authority separately. `bind()`, dry-binds, seat walks and assignment replay do not consult the lease. For same-repository callers, scope-touching non-holder lands refuse and code-only lands proceed, except for the stray-main-token refusal below. Corrupt authority refuses execution and Land regardless of footprint.

The persistent token is the mode-0600, ignored `.fgos/documentation-cutover.token` file in the holder checkout root. Gates hash the token read from the declared checkout, subject to the repository and stray-main checks. The sidecar stores its hash; argv, environment, Unit/assignment records and refusal messages do not carry the token. Within those checks, any process under the same OS user that can read that file can act as holder, including at `landRunnerItem`. This protects against accidents, not deliberate bypass. `--owner-confirmed` is an explicit owner assertion in this single-owner repository, not proof of a human or of holder death.

`git clean -fdX` deletes the ignored token. Losing it does not reopen the freeze; owner abandon is the recovery door. For release by a linked holder, the door temporarily lends its authenticated token to main's token path under main-50 so the commit hooks can check it. Normal success or failure restores main's previous bytes, removing the lent copy only if no file existed there before. A crash, SIGKILL or power loss before `finally` can leave that copy in main.

When a token file exists in main but main is not the recorded holder checkout, doctor fails and acquire refuses (error `stray-main-token`). While the lease is held, admission also refuses a main-checkout caller with that file as `stray-main-token`, before token-hash admission or any scoped, code-only or empty-path exception. The real linked holder can still release. Release removes its holder token after committing, but preserves any pre-existing stray main copy by restoring its previous bytes. After checking committed lease state and the recorded holder, the owner removes the stray main file by hand; no automatic residue cleanup is provided.

The `documentation-cutover-lease` doctor check diagnoses wiring, committed state, stray main tokens and the kernel lock resource; a held lease is a failing check with age. Held/corrupt authority still fails if the reference hook disappears. See the [doctor registry contract](../packaging-distribution/contracts/setup-doctor-registry.md#3-doctor-contract) for applicability. Release drift values are diagnostic evidence only. Cutover must recompute digests directly from Git and must never trust sidecar `drift` or `releaseScopeDigests` as authority.

Known limits:

- Corrupt committed sidecars also refuse no-op main maintenance transactions such as `pack-refs --all`/`gc`; owner-confirmed abandon/repair is the recovery door.
- Composite Work-item/fanout dispatch can `pick` (claim/create a worktree) before `runUnit` refuses. Claim worktrees have no holder token, so even a holder's Work-item dispatch through them refuses. The execution-door check does not undo the earlier claim/worktree effects.
- Legacy pre-case runs resumed without a held lease may record the resumer's checkout as origin on first case creation. During a held lease, missing recorded origin falls back to main and cannot gain holder identity from a later caller's token-bearing checkout. No retroactive origin correction is provided.

Implementation: [lease module](../../../src/runner/documentation-cutover-lease.mjs). The Node facade takes locks, probes, drains and lists holders in process through the `holderLock` namespace of the combined addon (Linux and macOS; Windows keeps `lock-hold`), as the Git component's loan already did with its one-shot capability; the lock-fd route modes that served it are deleted and only `--borrowed-check` and `--shared-try` stay for the git hook. The checkout channel (`node bin/fgos.mjs`) is unsupported for the lock verbs and the `state-root` route and its Node fallback are removed: the state root is the host's pin, else the door's answer over the same Rust formula. The cutover fences and their doctor row and fix are removed under the one-release policy, the key `lock.predecessorKillWaitMs` and its row are removed (the kill wait is fixed at 2000 ms), and `lock-record-unreadable` and `state-root` merge into `lock-holders` and `lock-kernel-semantics`, so the registered `lock-*` rows are three and no condition is lost. Bounded in-process blocking (section 9) and the Windows release limit (section 15) are the two accepted limits. Reused: the Git loan precedent (capability, External, marks); deleted: `fences.mjs`, the registry fence columns, three route modes' Node callers.

Coordinator then selected table-first positive detection plus the inode-checked shared-probe fallback, accepting its brief Try-contention window (§5). Exclusive Linux `release` and `Drop` share that settle; borrows/admission retain one lagged `Since` pass and refuse missing creation marks rather than using a full scan. Full descriptor scans remain only for uncertain release/leaks and Node's unknown-history drain. Unreadable facts never imply clearance. The component reuses process identities, fdinfo parsing and a shared kill/wait loop; no persistent pid ownership or kept duplicate. See [counsel](../../../plans/reports/counsel-261019-0204-holder-lock-release-settle.md) and [implementation evidence](../../../plans/reports/phase-lead-261019-0204-git-perf-release-settle.md).

Component Classes","sectionText":"#### 1. Component Classes

Invocation mechanism describes how an implementation is invoked. It does not describe the product nature, release ownership, or authority posture of the component being invoked — that is a separate axis, **component class**:

```txt
component class    -> who owns/releases/configures the component
invocation mechanism -> how the selected provider is invoked at runtime
```

A `ProviderDescriptor` therefore declares both: component class (core, packaged extension, or user plugin) and invocation mechanism (built-in, legacy node, external process, or external WASM).

Component Protocol","sectionText":"#### 3. Component Protocol

The semantic component protocol is versioned independently from public host protocols — `fgos.component.v1`, distinct from CLI `fgos.v1` and any remote API version. It carries: operation identity and protocol/schema version range; request ID and optional parent/correlation ID; typed request, result, and error payloads; deadline, cancellation, progress, and events where supported; capability context granted by the host; provider identity and diagnostics needed for tracing.

For process plugins, version one uses JSON-RPC 2.0 semantics over 4-byte big-endian length-prefixed UTF-8 JSON frames on stdio. Newline-delimited JSON is not the contract: a length prefix gives one enforceable maximum-frame boundary and does not make embedded or future formatted content ambiguous. Stdout is protocol only; logs go to stderr or a declared log notification.

The host starts a process only after static manifest selection. Its first exchange confirms provider identity, accepted manifest digest, component protocol range, supported operation/contract pairs, and concurrency limit. Discovery never depends on this handshake; a mismatch terminates the provider and fails closed.

One connection obeys these lifecycle rules:

- request IDs are unique per connection;
- responses may complete out of order only when concurrency greater than one was negotiated;
- requests, frames, and event queues are bounded to provide backpressure;
- cancellation sends a protocol notification, waits a bounded grace period, then terminates the provider process if necessary;
- cancellation acknowledgement does not claim semantic side effects were rolled back;
- a crash after dispatch yields completion-unknown unless the operation's idempotency contract and key explicitly permit retry;
- a one-shot CLI may own one process for its lifetime; a gateway may pool or persist connections under the adapter's health/restart policy.
